intro: Chopin’s Étude in E minor, Op. 25 No. 5, marked Vivace, is built on quick semitone clashes, and its middle section is an E major melody in the low register of the piano. Edward Neeman plays.

sections.label: A · Semitone clashes and short chords
sections.mNote: Quick dissonances break into light, scherzando piano writing.

sections.label: B · Left-hand melody in E major
sections.mNote: A low melody under rising and falling figures in the right hand.

sections.label: A′ · E minor, opening material returns
sections.mNote: The broken rhythms and quick clashes return after the middle section.

sections.label: Coda · E major, fortissimo
sections.mNote: Full chords and an upward flourish close in E major.

cues.title: Semitone clashes, right hand
cues.text: The right hand repeatedly sounds notes a semitone apart, which produces quick minor-second clashes against the E minor theme. Chopin marked the music scherzando (joking) and broke its phrases into short, lightly played gestures.
cues.evidence: Minor-second dissonances: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._25,_No._5_(Chopin). Vivace, scherzando and broken rhythms: Mieczysław Tomaszewski, https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Più lento in E major
cues.text: The Più lento is slower and in E major. The melody moves to the left hand, in the range of a cello, while the right hand plays rising and falling figuration above it.
cues.evidence: E-major Più lento: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._25,_No._5_(Chopin). Cello-register melody and accompanying figuration: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedication of Op. 25, 1837
cues.text: The twelve études of Op. 25 appeared in 1837 with a dedication to Marie d’Agoult, the companion of Chopin’s friend Franz Liszt.
cues.evidence: IMSLP, Études, Op. 25: first published 1837 (Paris: Maurice Schlesinger), dedicated to Comtesse d’Agoult (1805–1876): https://imslp.org/wiki/Études,_Op.25_(Chopin,_Frédéric). Liszt’s relationship with Marie d’Agoult from 1834: https://www.liszt.org/p/chronology.html

cues.title: Sitsky’s First Piano Sonata
cues.text: Larry Sitsky, one of Neeman’s teachers, wrote his First Piano Sonata for him. Neeman made its first recording on his debut album of 2016, where it appeared alongside Rachmaninoff.
cues.evidence: Australian National University biography: Sitsky as teacher, the dedicated Sonata No. 1 and Neeman’s March 2016 debut album Rachmaninoff & Sitsky. https://music.cass.anu.edu.au/people/dr-edward-neeman

cues.title: Return of the opening section
cues.text: The opening in E minor returns at its quicker pace. The low melodic line stops, and the piano resumes its broken rhythms and brief dissonances. The hands play short exchanges.
cues.evidence: Return of the scherzando outer section after the slower trio: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191 and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._25,_No._5_(Chopin).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda in E major
cues.text: At the end the dynamic rises sharply. Fortissimo chords and an ascending passage take the piano into E major, the key of the middle section. Both hands play at full strength in the closing bars.
cues.evidence: Tomaszewski describes the dramatic final turn, fortissimo chords and ascending major-key passage. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Più lento in E major
transitions.from: A · Semitone clashes and short chords
transitions.to: B · Left-hand melody in E major
transitions.how: The E minor scherzando closes and the Più lento begins in E major. The left hand plays a sustained melody in the cello’s range. The right hand plays rising and falling figures in place of the clipped chords and semitone clashes of the opening.
transitions.evidence: Slower middle and cello-register melody: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191. Più lento and E major: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._25,_No._5_(Chopin).

transitions.title: Return of the E minor opening
transitions.from: B · Left-hand melody in E major
transitions.to: A′ · E minor, opening material returns
transitions.how: The E major section closes, and the quick E minor opening returns. The left hand gives up its long melody, and the piano resumes the short broken chords and semitone dissonances. The marking scherzando again applies to the clipped exchange between the hands.
transitions.evidence: The étude’s scherzo-and-trio design and return: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191 and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._25,_No._5_(Chopin).

transitions.title: Coda in E major
transitions.from: A′ · E minor, opening material returns
transitions.how: The E minor scherzando music returns and leads into a forceful coda. Fortissimo chords and a rising flourish on the piano establish E major, the key of the middle section.
transitions.evidence: Final fortissimo chords and major-key flourish: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191.

composer.born: 1 March 1810, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
